Paleomagnetic results from the Singhbhum Craton, India: Remagnetization,
demagnetization, and complication
Anthony F. Pivarunasa,*, Joseph G. Meerta, Karastin D. Katusina, Manoj K. Panditb,
Scott R. Millera, Aubrey Cravera, Kelli M. Roderusa, Anup Sinhac
aUniversity of Florida, Department of Geological Sciences, 241 Williamson Hall, Gainesville, FL 32611
bDepartment of Geology, University of Rajasthan, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India
cGeomagnetic Research Laboratory, Regional Center of Indian Institute of Geomagnetism, Allahabad, 221 505, India
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: We report a complicated magnetic fidelity through time in Singhbhum Craton, India, with new, geographically
Paleomagnetism wide-spread and spatially detailed, paleomagnetic results. The Singhbhum Craton in eastern India is cross-cut by
Singhbhum multiple generations of the so-called “Newer Dolerite” dykes. A previously published 1765 Ma paleomagnetic
Craton
pole represents a useful constraint on the Singhbhum Craton during the amalgamation of the Columbia super-
India
continent whereas an older ~2763 Ma paleomagnetic pole is problematic. We present additional data from the
Proterozoic 1765 Ma dykes that results in a grand mean paleomagnetic pole at 43◦N, 320◦E (A95 =10◦, K =17; N =13). The
Dykes
1765 Ma pole is supported by a positive baked contact test. Our additional data shows that paleomagnetic results
from the 1765 Ma dykes are more complicated by magnetic overprints than originally reported. We also argue
that the steep inclination paleomagnetic data from the Singhbhum Craton, previously assumed to represent a
Neoarchean signal, are part of a complicated group whose magnetic age is uncertain. We establish a minimum
age of 2250 Ma for connecting the Singhbhum and Dharwar cratons on the basis of published geochronology and
our interpretation of paleomagnetic data in this paper. Paleomagnetic data from both cratons can be juxtaposed
using a simple Euler pole rotation of the Singhbhum Craton relative to Dharwar.

Fig. 2. Simplified geological map (GSI 1:2M Map, 1998) of Singhbhum Craton and sampling sites, line segments indicating dyke trends as determined via field
observations and satellite imagery. Radiometrically dated dykes are indicated by stars. Heavily sampled areas which lack detail on this scale are indicated as KR –
Kanjhari Reservoir and BK – Bhima Kunda. They are detailed with finer-scale mapping in the Supplementary Material associated with this paper. BG =Bonai Granite.
Other units as labeled, geology is approximate. Inset map to the top left indicates location of Singhbhum Craton within major provinces of peninsular India: SC:
Singhbhum Craton, BC: Bastar Craton, DC: Dharwar Craton, SGT: Southern Granulite Terrain, DT: Deccan Traps, AC: Aravalli Craton, BuC: Bundelkhand Craton.

4.2. Steeply-inclined dual polarity magnetic data 4.2.1. Singhbhum paleomagnetic group 1 (SPG1)
Paleomagnetic results from 19 dykes (24 sites) in Singhbhum Craton

to steeply inclined directions that were isolated in our study; hereafter steeply down or SW-steeply up magnetic vectors (Fig. 7). These dykes
